qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
GROWING UP WITH GRANDPARENTS
In Viet Nam, it is common for three generations to live under one roof. Grandparents often look after young children while their parents are at work. This arrangement has clear advantages. Children receive constant care from people who love them, and parents can focus on their jobs without paying for childcare. Grandparents, in turn, feel useful and less lonely.
However, living together is not always easy. Grandparents may have different ideas about raising children. For example, they might give children more sweets or allow them to watch television for longer than parents would like. Such differences can lead to tension in the family.
Experts suggest that open communication is the key. Parents should explain their rules politely, and grandparents should respect the parents' decisions. When both sides listen to each other, children benefit from the wisdom of the old and the energy of the young.
In recent years, more young couples have moved to big cities and live in small flats. As a result, the number of extended families is decreasing. Still, many people believe that the close relationship between grandparents and grandchildren is a valuable part of Vietnamese culture that should be preserved.
qs.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as an advantage of living with grandparents?

qs.ex: “This arrangement” chỉ việc ba thế hệ sống chung và ông bà trông cháu.

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
THE CHANGING ROLE OF FATHERS
[I] Not long ago, the father in a typical family was seen mainly as the breadwinner. [II] He went out to work, earned money and made the important decisions, while the mother took care of the home and the children. [III] Today, this picture is changing quickly. [IV]
One reason is that more women now have full-time jobs. When both parents earn an income, it no longer makes sense for one person to do all the housework. Many fathers now cook, clean and take their children to school. Some even choose to stay at home while their wives continue their careers. These 'stay-at-home dads' were rare a generation ago, but they are becoming more accepted.
Another reason is a growing understanding of how important fathers are to children's development. Studies show that children whose fathers are actively involved in their lives tend to have higher self-esteem and better social skills. They are also more likely to do well at school. As this research has spread, many men have begun to see childcare not as 'women's work' but as a responsibility they share.
Of course, change does not happen overnight. Some fathers still feel embarrassed to take paternity leave, and some workplaces do not support them. In addition, traditional attitudes remain strong in certain communities, where people may criticise men who do housework.
Nevertheless, the trend is clear. The modern father is no longer just a provider; he is also a carer, a teacher and a friend. This shift benefits not only children but also fathers themselves, who often say that spending more time with their families makes their lives more meaningful.

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
THE GRATITUDE JAR
Last New Year's Eve, the Pham family in Hai Phong opened a large glass jar that had been sitting on their bookshelf all year. Inside were more than two hundred small pieces of paper, each one describing something a family member was thankful for.
The idea came from twelve-year-old Vy, who had seen it in a video. At first, her older brother thought it was silly. 'I didn't want to write about my feelings,' he admits. But after a few weeks, he began adding notes too – thanking his mother for waiting up when he came home late and his sister for lending him her calculator.
Reading the notes together turned out to be the highlight of the year. Some made the family laugh, such as Dad's note thanking the cat for not breaking anything that week. Others brought tears to their eyes. Grandmother had written, 'I am thankful that my grandchildren still ask me to tell stories.'
Mrs Pham says the jar has changed the atmosphere at home. 'We notice the good things more,' she explains. 'When you know you're going to write a note, you start paying attention to small acts of kindness.' This year, the family has started a new jar – and Vy's brother was the first to add a note.
qs.q: When did the Pham family open the jar?

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
PASSING VALUES DOWN THE GENERATIONS
[I] Every family passes something on to its children – not only possessions, but also values and beliefs. [II] These values shape how young people think about work, money, relationships and their duties to others. [III] Most of this learning happens not through lectures but through everyday example. [IV]
In Viet Nam, many families place great importance on filial piety – the duty of children to respect and care for their parents. This value is reflected in daily life: children greet their elders politely, adult children often support their ageing parents, and families gather to honour their ancestors on special occasions.
Hard work and education are also highly valued. Many grandparents who grew up in poverty encourage their grandchildren to study hard so that they can have better opportunities. For these older generations, education is seen as the most reliable path to a secure future.
However, globalisation and technology have introduced new values. Today's young people are often more individualistic and more willing to question tradition. They may choose careers based on personal interest rather than family expectations, or decide to live independently before marriage.
These differences can create tension, but they can also enrich family life. When grandparents share their experiences and young people share their perspectives, each generation learns from the other. In the end, the values that survive are those that families continue to discuss, adapt and practise together.
qs.q:
Where in paragraph 1 does the following sentence best fit?
“Children watch how their parents treat others and learn from what they see.”

qs.p:
A BIG FAMILY UNDER ONE ROOF
Nine-year-old Bao lives in Hue with his parents, his younger sister, his grandparents and his uncle's family. With eleven people in one house, daily life is never quiet. Yet Bao says he would not want it any other way.
Each morning, Bao's grandmother gets up first to go to the market. His mother and aunt take turns cooking breakfast, while the men are in charge of cleaning the yard and repairing anything that is broken. The children's jobs are smaller but still important: Bao feeds the chickens, and his cousins set the table.
Living in such a large household requires patience. There is often a queue for the bathroom, and the television is the subject of frequent disagreements. However, the family has a simple rule: problems are discussed at dinner, where everyone, including the children, can give their opinion.
Bao's grandfather believes that living together helps to keep family traditions alive. He teaches the children old folk songs and tells them stories about the family's history. 'When I am gone,' he says, 'they will remember where they came from.'
qs.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as living in Bao's house?

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
o: Folk songs are no longer useful.
Children should move to big cities.
Living together keeps family traditions alive.
qs.p:
A BIG FAMILY UNDER ONE ROOF
Nine-year-old Bao lives in Hue with his parents, his younger sister, his grandparents and his uncle's family. With eleven people in one house, daily life is never quiet. Yet Bao says he would not want it any other way.
Each morning, Bao's grandmother gets up first to go to the market. His mother and aunt take turns cooking breakfast, while the men are in charge of cleaning the yard and repairing anything that is broken. The children's jobs are smaller but still important: Bao feeds the chickens, and his cousins set the table.
Living in such a large household requires patience. There is often a queue for the bathroom, and the television is the subject of frequent disagreements. However, the family has a simple rule: problems are discussed at dinner, where everyone, including the children, can give their opinion.
Bao's grandfather believes that living together helps to keep family traditions alive. He teaches the children old folk songs and tells them stories about the family's history. 'When I am gone,' he says, 'they will remember where they came from.'
qs.q: What does Bao's grandfather believe?

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
SAYING THANK YOU AT HOME
[I] We are taught to say 'thank you' to shop assistants, waiters and strangers who hold the door for us. [II] Yet at home, the people who do the most for us often hear these words the least. [III] Many of us take our family members' efforts for granted. [IV]
Psychologists say that this lack of appreciation can slowly damage relationships. When a mother cooks dinner every evening without hearing a word of thanks, she may start to feel that her work is invisible. Over time, she may become tired and resentful, even if she loves her family deeply.
On the other hand, expressing gratitude has powerful effects. Studies of couples and families have found that people who feel appreciated are more willing to help others and less likely to argue. Gratitude also benefits the person who expresses it. Those who regularly notice the good things others do for them tend to feel happier and more satisfied with their lives.
Fortunately, showing appreciation does not require much time or money. A simple 'thank you' after a meal, a short note left on the table or a hug at the end of a long day can make a real difference. Some families keep a 'thank-you board' in the kitchen where members write messages to one another.
Teenagers in particular may find it awkward to express their feelings. But small habits, practised every day, can gradually change the atmosphere of a home. As one family counsellor puts it, 'Gratitude is like water for a plant: a little, given regularly, keeps a relationship alive.'

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
o: has become usual, especially in cities
qs.p:
NUCLEAR OR EXTENDED?
In the past, most Vietnamese people lived in extended families, with three or even four generations under one roof. Today, especially in cities, the nuclear family – parents and their children – has become the norm. Each type of family has its own strengths.
In an extended family, there is always someone to help. Grandparents can look after babies, and household chores are shared among many adults. Children also learn respect for older people and absorb family traditions naturally. However, privacy can be limited, and disagreements between generations are common.
A nuclear family, on the other hand, usually enjoys more independence. Parents can make decisions about their children's education and lifestyle without interference. Homes are quieter, and each person often has more personal space. The disadvantage is that parents may feel overloaded, especially when both of them work full-time and there is no one to help with childcare.
Many families today are finding a middle way. They live separately from their parents but nearby, visiting several times a week. In this way, they keep their independence while still enjoying the support and warmth of a larger family.
qs.q: According to paragraph 1, the nuclear family ___.

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
A WEEK AS THE HOMEMAKER
[I] Last month, our class took part in an unusual experiment. [II] For one week, each of us had to swap roles with the person who does most of the housework in our home. [III] For many of us, that person was our mother. [IV]
I thought the challenge would be easy. After all, how hard could it be to cook a few meals and do some cleaning? By Tuesday, I had changed my mind. I woke up at 5.30 to go to the market, prepared breakfast for five people and still had to get to school on time. In the evening, there were dishes to wash, clothes to fold and my little brother's homework to check.
The hardest part was not the physical work but the planning. I had to think about what to cook, what we had run out of and how much money was left for the week. My mother does all of this without a list, while also working part-time at a pharmacy.
On Friday, I burnt the rice and forgot to buy milk. My father laughed, but my mother simply hugged me and said, 'Now you know.' I did know. I had never really noticed how much she did for us, because she always did it quietly.
Since the experiment ended, things have changed in our house. We now have a weekly chore chart, and everyone, including my father, has regular tasks. My mother says she finally has time to read in the evenings, something she had not done for years. For me, the experiment was a lesson in gratitude that no textbook could have taught.
qs.q:

“Only a few students named their father or a grandparent.”

I woke up at 5.30 to go to the market, prepared breakfast for five people and still had to get to school on time. In the evening, there were dishes to wash, clothes to fold and my little brother's homework to check.
The hardest part was not the physical work but the planning. I had to think about what to cook, what we had run out of and how much money was left for the week. My mother does all of this without a list, while also working part-time at a pharmacy.
On Friday, I burnt the rice and forgot to buy milk. My father laughed, but my mother simply hugged me and said, 'Now you know.' I did know. I had never really noticed how much she did for us, because she always did it quietly.
Since the experiment ended, things have changed in our house. We now have a weekly chore chart, and everyone, including my father, has regular tasks. My mother says she finally has time to read in the evenings, something she had not done for years. For me, the experiment was a lesson in gratitude that no textbook could have taught.
qs.q: What can be inferred about the writer's mother before the experiment?

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.

qs.p:
WHEN MUM IS THE BREADWINNER
Ten years ago, Mrs Lan's husband had a serious accident and could no longer work full-time. Since then, she has been the main breadwinner for her family of four. She runs a small clothing business in Da Nang and often works more than ten hours a day.
At first, the change was difficult for everyone. Mr Hung felt embarrassed that his wife earned more than he did, and some neighbours made unkind comments. But gradually, the family found a new balance. Mr Hung took over most of the housework: he cooks, cleans and takes the children to school. He says he has become much closer to his son and daughter as a result.
Their story is not unusual. According to recent surveys, a growing number of Vietnamese women earn as much as or more than their husbands. Sociologists say this reflects women's improved access to education and jobs.
For Mrs Lan, the most important thing is not who earns the money but how the family works together. 'We are a team,' she says. 'Everyone does what they can, and nobody's job is less important.'
qs.q: Why did Mrs Lan become the main breadwinner?

qs.p:
HOUSEWORK ACROSS GENERATIONS
[I] Ask your grandparents about housework when they were young, and you will probably hear very different stories from your own. [II] Fifty years ago, most families had no washing machines, fridges or rice cookers. [III] Clothes were washed by hand in the river or a large basin, and meals were cooked over wood or coal fires. [IV]
In those days, housework was also divided strictly by gender. Women were expected to cook, clean and raise children, while men worked in the fields or earned money outside the home. A man seen washing dishes might have been laughed at by his neighbours.
Today, the situation is quite different. Household appliances have reduced the amount of physical labour needed, and attitudes have shifted. In many young families, husbands and wives share chores more equally, and it is no longer unusual to see a father cooking dinner or hanging out the washing.

qs.p:
CHORES AND FUTURE SUCCESS
Can washing dishes as a child help you succeed as an adult? According to a number of long-term studies, the answer may be yes. Researchers who followed people from childhood into middle age found that those who had done regular chores were more likely to have successful careers and good relationships.
Why might this be? Experts suggest that chores teach children a 'pitch-in' mindset: the understanding that when something needs to be done, you do it without waiting to be asked. This attitude is highly valued by employers, who look for workers able to take the initiative and cooperate with colleagues.
Chores also help children develop self-discipline. Making your bed every morning or feeding a pet every evening may seem trivial, but such habits train young people to keep commitments even when they would rather do something else.
Despite these benefits, many modern parents excuse their children from housework so that they can concentrate on schoolwork and extra classes. Experts warn that this may be a mistake. Academic success matters, they say, but so do the practical and social skills that children learn by contributing to the life of their home.

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
SINGLE PARENTS, STRONG FAMILIES
[I] In Viet Nam, as in many countries, the number of single-parent families has been rising. [II] Some parents raise their children alone after divorce, while others have lost a partner through illness or accident. [III] Whatever the reason, single parents face challenges that two-parent families may never experience. [IV]
The most obvious challenge is time. A single parent must often be both the breadwinner and the homemaker, working full-time while also cooking, cleaning and helping with homework. Money can also be a problem, since the family depends on one income. Many single parents report feeling exhausted and isolated.
Yet research shows that children from single-parent families can do just as well as their peers. What matters most is not the number of parents but the quality of the relationship and the stability of daily life. Children who feel loved, have clear routines and receive support from relatives or friends tend to thrive.
In fact, many children of single parents develop strengths at an early age. Because they share more responsibilities at home, they often become independent, resourceful and mature. 'My son learnt to cook at nine,' says Ms Thu, a nurse in Can Tho who has raised her child alone. 'Now, at sixteen, he is the one who reminds me to rest.'
Communities can help by offering flexible working hours, affordable childcare and simple kindness. A neighbour who picks a child up from school once a week may not seem to be doing much, but for a busy single parent, such help can make an enormous difference.
qs.q:

“Each of these situations brings its own difficulties.”

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
SHOULD CHILDREN BE PAID FOR CHORES?
Few topics divide parents as much as pocket money. In particular, should children be paid for helping at home?
Supporters of paying for chores believe it teaches children about the real world. In adult life, people are paid for their work, so why should children be different? Earning money also gives children a chance to learn how to save, budget and make decisions about spending. A teenager who has worked hard for a pair of trainers is likely to value them more than one who received them as a gift.
Opponents argue that paying for chores sends the wrong message. Housework, they say, is a shared responsibility that comes with being part of a family. If children are paid to tidy their rooms, they may refuse to help unless there is a reward. 'What's in it for me?' is not the attitude parents want to encourage.
Many families choose a combination of both approaches. Basic tasks such as making the bed or clearing the table are expected of everyone without payment. Extra jobs, like washing the car or helping with a family business, can earn a small amount of money. This system rewards effort while keeping the idea that everyone contributes to the home.
qs.q: According to paragraph 1, pocket money is a topic that ___.

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
THE QUIET STRENGTH OF THE HOMEMAKER
[I] For much of the twentieth century, being a homemaker was considered the natural role for women in many societies. [II] Advertisements showed smiling housewives with shiny new kitchen appliances, suggesting that a clean home was a woman's greatest achievement. [III] Yet behind these images lay long hours of unpaid and often unrecognised work. [IV]
Economists have tried to calculate the value of this work. If homemakers were paid market wages for cooking, cleaning, childcare and caring for the elderly, their annual salary would be considerable. In some countries, estimates suggest that unpaid household work is equal to a large proportion of the national economy.
In recent decades, the image of the homemaker has changed. More women have entered the workforce, and more men have chosen to stay at home and care for their families. The term 'homemaker' itself has become gender-neutral, describing anyone who manages a household.
Nevertheless, homemakers still struggle for recognition. Many report feeling undervalued when people ask, 'So, what do you do all day?' Some countries have responded by offering pensions or tax benefits to full-time carers, acknowledging that their contribution to society is real.
Perhaps the greatest change needed is in attitudes. Running a home requires organisation, patience, problem-solving and emotional intelligence – skills that are highly valued in any workplace. Recognising this may help us appreciate the people who keep our homes, and our families, running smoothly.
qs.q:
Where in paragraph 1 does the following sentence best fit?
“Few people stopped to ask whether this work deserved more respect.”

o: our first friends and our first rivals
qs.p:
BROTHERS AND SISTERS
Siblings are often our first friends – and our first rivals. Growing up together, brothers and sisters share bedrooms, toys and their parents' attention. It is no surprise that conflict is common. Some studies suggest that young siblings argue several times every hour they spend together!
However, these arguments are not always harmful. Through them, children learn how to negotiate, compromise and see situations from another person's point of view. In a sense, the family home is a training ground for social skills that children will need later in life.
Birth order may also play a role in shaping personality, although scientists disagree about how strong this effect is. Older children are sometimes described as responsible and ambitious, while younger ones are said to be more relaxed and sociable. Critics point out that many other factors, such as gender and family size, matter just as much.
What is clear is that sibling relationships usually last longer than any other. Brothers and sisters often remain close long after their parents have passed away. As adults, many say that their siblings are the people who understand them best, because they share the same memories of childhood.

qs.p:
SMART HOMES: WILL ROBOTS DO OUR CHORES?
[I] Imagine coming home to find the floors already vacuumed, the laundry folded and dinner cooking itself. [II] For some families, this scene is no longer science fiction. [III] Robot vacuum cleaners, smart washing machines and automatic cookers are now found in many homes around the world. [IV]
Supporters of smart home technology say it frees up valuable time. Instead of spending hours on cleaning and cooking, family members can relax, exercise or spend time together. For elderly people and those with disabilities, smart devices can also make independent living easier and safer.
However, critics raise several concerns. Smart devices can be expensive, and not every family can afford them. They also collect data about people's daily habits, raising questions about privacy. Furthermore, if machines do everything, children may grow up without learning basic life skills such as cooking a simple meal or sewing on a button.
There is also an emotional side to housework that machines cannot replace. Cooking a favourite dish for someone you love or teaching a child to fold clothes are acts of care. Some psychologists argue that doing chores together strengthens family bonds in a way that pressing a button never could.
The future will probably involve a balance. Technology can take over the most tiring and repetitive tasks, while families continue to share the meaningful ones. After all, a home is not just a place that is kept clean – it is a place where people care for one another.
qs.q:
Where in paragraph 1 does the following sentence best fit?
“Many of them can even be controlled from a smartphone.”

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
LEARNING TO LIVE ALONE
When Huong moved to Ha Noi to study at university, she was excited about her new freedom. Within a week, however, she realised how unprepared she was. She had never used a washing machine, could only cook instant noodles and had no idea how to manage her monthly allowance.
'At home, my mother did everything,' she admits. 'I just studied.' By the end of the first month, Huong had run out of money, her white shirts had turned pink in the wash, and she was surviving on bread and milk.
Her story is common among first-year students. University counsellors say that many young people struggle not with their studies but with everyday tasks. Some become so stressed that their grades suffer.
Huong eventually asked her roommate for help. Together, they made a weekly budget and a cooking schedule. Huong also called her mother every evening to learn simple recipes. Six months later, she can cook a dozen dishes and has even started saving money.
Her advice to younger students is clear: 'Learn to look after yourself before you leave home. Your parents won't always be there to do it for you.'
qs.q: How did Huong feel when she first moved to Ha Noi?

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
WHY FAMILY TRADITIONS MATTER
[I] Every family has its own traditions, from special birthday breakfasts to annual trips to the grandparents' village. [II] Some are passed down through many generations, while others are created by accident. [III] Whatever their origin, these rituals play an important role in family life. [IV]
Psychologists say that traditions give children a sense of identity and belonging. Knowing that their family always makes banh xeo on the first rainy day of the year, for example, helps children feel part of something larger than themselves. This sense of belonging has been linked to higher self-esteem and better mental health.
Traditions also provide stability in times of change. When a family moves house, welcomes a new baby or loses a loved one, familiar rituals offer comfort and continuity. They remind family members that, although some things change, the family itself remains.
Moreover, traditions create shared memories. Years later, adults often remember family rituals more clearly than expensive gifts or holidays. A father who read stories to his children every night may discover that, for them, those evenings were the best part of childhood.
Creating new traditions is easy and inexpensive. A weekly game night, a monthly picnic or even a special way of saying goodbye can become meaningful over time. What matters is not how elaborate the tradition is but that it is repeated and enjoyed together.
qs.q:
Where in paragraph 1 does the following sentence best fit?
“Either way, they help to make each family unique.”

Psychologists say that traditions give children a sense of identity and belonging. Knowing that their family always makes banh xeo on the first rainy day of the year, for example, helps children feel part of something larger than themselves. This sense of belonging has been linked to higher self-esteem and better mental health.
Traditions also provide stability in times of change. When a family moves house, welcomes a new baby or loses a loved one, familiar rituals offer comfort and continuity. They remind family members that, although some things change, the family itself remains.
Moreover, traditions create shared memories. Years later, adults often remember family rituals more clearly than expensive gifts or holidays. A father who read stories to his children every night may discover that, for them, those evenings were the best part of childhood.
Creating new traditions is easy and inexpensive. A weekly game night, a monthly picnic or even a special way of saying goodbye can become meaningful over time. What matters is not how elaborate the tradition is but that it is repeated and enjoyed together.

He lost his job at the bank.
His wife was offered a better-paid job with long hours.
qs.p:
THE STAY-AT-HOME DAD
When Mr Khanh's wife was offered a promotion in Ho Chi Minh City, the couple faced a difficult decision. Her new job paid much more than his, but it required long hours. After many discussions, they agreed that Mr Khanh would leave his job as a bank clerk and stay at home with their two young sons.
The first months were challenging. Mr Khanh had rarely cooked before, and he found it hard to manage the children's schedules. Some relatives criticised him, saying that a man should be the breadwinner. Even at the playground, he was often the only father among dozens of mothers.
Gradually, however, he gained confidence. He learnt to cook from online videos, started a small vegetable garden on the balcony and joined an online group of stay-at-home fathers who share advice and support. His sons, now six and eight, say their father makes the best fried rice in the world.
Mr Khanh admits that he sometimes misses his old job. But he says that the experience has changed his understanding of family life. 'I used to think housework was easy,' he says. 'Now I know it is a full-time job – and one of the most important ones there is.'
qs.q: Why did the couple decide that Mr Khanh should stay at home?

The first months were challenging. Mr Khanh had rarely cooked before, and he found it hard to manage the children's schedules. Some relatives criticised him, saying that a man should be the breadwinner. Even at the playground, he was often the only father among dozens of mothers.
Gradually, however, he gained confidence. He learnt to cook from online videos, started a small vegetable garden on the balcony and joined an online group of stay-at-home fathers who share advice and support. His sons, now six and eight, say their father makes the best fried rice in the world.
Mr Khanh admits that he sometimes misses his old job. But he says that the experience has changed his understanding of family life. 'I used to think housework was easy,' he says. 'Now I know it is a full-time job – and one of the most important ones there is.'

qs.p:
HOUSEHOLD CHORES AROUND THE WORLD
[I] How much children help at home varies greatly from one culture to another. [II] In some places, children are expected to contribute from the age of three or four. [III] In others, they are given few responsibilities until they are teenagers. [IV]
In some communities in Latin America, researchers have observed that young children often help without being asked. They notice what adults are doing and join in, whether it is cooking, sweeping or caring for younger siblings. Researchers believe this is because children in these communities are included in adult activities from an early age, rather than being kept separate.
In Japan, schoolchildren clean their own classrooms and serve lunch to their classmates. This practice teaches cooperation and respect for shared spaces. Many Japanese parents also give their children regular household tasks.
In contrast, studies in some wealthy countries have found that children spend little time on chores. Busy schedules filled with lessons, sports and homework leave little room for housework, and some parents feel that it is quicker to do the work themselves.
Experts suggest that all families can learn from the cultures where children help willingly. The key, they say, is to invite children to take part in real tasks alongside adults, rather than giving them artificial jobs or offering rewards. When children feel that their help genuinely matters, they are more likely to want to contribute.

“These differences reflect each society's beliefs about childhood.”

o: The brain stores information in long-term memory.
Information from the day is deleted.
qs.p:
THE POWER OF SLEEP
Many teenagers believe that sleeping less gives them more time to study. In reality, the opposite is true. Sleep plays a vital role in learning. During deep sleep, the brain organises the information collected during the day and stores it in long-term memory. Without enough sleep, students find it harder to concentrate and remember what they have learnt.
Lack of sleep also affects physical health. It weakens the immune system, making people more likely to catch colds and other infections. Over time, it can increase the risk of obesity, because tired people tend to crave sugary and fatty foods.
So why do so many young people sleep too little? One major reason is the use of smartphones at night. The blue light from screens tricks the brain into thinking it is still daytime, which delays the release of sleep hormones. In addition, endless social media updates keep users awake long after they intended to sleep.
Fortunately, there are simple ways to improve sleep. Experts advise keeping a regular bedtime, even at weekends, and switching off all screens at least an hour before bed. A quiet, dark and cool bedroom also helps. By making these small changes, students can wake up feeling refreshed and ready to learn.
qs.q: According to paragraph 1, what happens during deep sleep?

qs.i: Read the following passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D to indicate the best answer to each of the questions.
qs.p:
BLUE ZONES: LESSONS FROM THE WORLD'S LONGEST-LIVED PEOPLE
[I] Around the world, there are a few special places where people live much longer than average. [II] Researchers call them 'Blue Zones'. [III] They include Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy and Nicoya in Costa Rica. [IV]
Although these communities are far apart, their residents share several habits. First, they move naturally throughout the day. Instead of going to the gym, they walk, garden and do housework. Second, they eat mainly plant-based diets, with beans, vegetables and whole grains forming the core of most meals. Meat is eaten only occasionally, often just a few times a month.
Social connections are another key factor. In Okinawa, for example, people form lifelong groups of friends called 'moai', who support one another both emotionally and financially. Older people in Blue Zones are respected and usually live with or near their families, which gives them a strong sense of purpose.
Interestingly, people in these regions also have effective ways of dealing with stress. Some pray, some take short naps, and others simply enjoy a cup of tea with friends at sunset. Scientists believe that reducing stress lowers inflammation in the body, which is linked to many age-related diseases.
The lessons from Blue Zones are surprisingly simple. Living longer does not depend on expensive treatments or special supplements. Rather, it depends on everyday choices: staying active, eating sensibly, keeping close relationships and finding time to relax. Anyone, anywhere, can adopt these habits.

[I] Around the world, there are a few special places where people live much longer than average. [II] Researchers call them 'Blue Zones'. [III] They include Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy and Nicoya in Costa Rica. [IV]

Second, they eat mainly plant-based diets, with beans, vegetables and whole grains forming the core of most meals. Meat is eaten only occasionally, often just a few times a month.

Older people in Blue Zones are respected and usually live with or near their families, which gives them a strong sense of purpose.
Interestingly, people in these regions also have effective ways of dealing with stress. Some pray, some take short naps, and others simply enjoy a cup of tea with friends at sunset. Scientists believe that reducing stress lowers inflammation in the body, which is linked to many age-related diseases.

o: She had found a job at a hospital.
Women were not allowed to attend university in her country.
She wanted to join the army.
She wanted to meet Pierre Curie.
qs.p:
MARIE CURIE: A LIFE DEVOTED TO SCIENCE
Marie Curie was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867. At that time, women were not allowed to attend university in her country. Determined to continue her education, she moved to Paris in 1891 and studied physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne, often living on little more than bread and tea.
In Paris, she met Pierre Curie, a scientist who shared her passion for research. They married in 1895 and worked together on radioactivity, a term that Marie herself created. In 1903, the couple shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, making Marie the first woman ever to receive the award.
Tragedy struck in 1906 when Pierre was killed in a street accident. Despite her grief, Marie continued their work and took over his teaching post, becoming the first female professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911, she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for discovering the elements polonium and radium.
During the First World War, Curie developed mobile X-ray units to help doctors treat wounded soldiers. She even drove the vehicles to the front line herself. Sadly, years of working with radioactive materials damaged her health, and she died in 1934. Her notebooks are still so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes today.
qs.q: Why did Marie Curie move to Paris?

In Paris, she met Pierre Curie, a scientist who shared her passion for research. They married in 1895 and worked together on radioactivity, a term that Marie herself created. In 1903, the couple shared the Nobel Prize in Physics, making Marie the first woman ever to receive the award.
Tragedy struck in 1906 when Pierre was killed in a street accident. Despite her grief, Marie continued their work and took over his teaching post, becoming the first female professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911, she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for discovering the elements polonium and radium.
During the First World War, Curie developed mobile X-ray units to help doctors treat wounded soldiers. She even drove the vehicles to the front line herself. Sadly, years of working with radioactive materials damaged her health, and she died in 1934. Her notebooks are still so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes today.

DANG THUY TRAM AND HER DIARY
[I] Dang Thuy Tram was born in 1942 into a family of doctors in Ha Noi. [II] After graduating from medical school, she volunteered to work in a field hospital in Quang Ngai province during the war. [III] There she treated wounded soldiers and local people, often in extremely difficult conditions. [IV]
Throughout those years, Tram kept a diary. In it, she wrote about her patients, her longing for her family and her dreams of peace. She also recorded her doubts and fears with remarkable honesty. Her words reveal not a perfect hero but a young woman who was sensitive, idealistic and deeply caring.
In 1970, Tram was killed while she was still in her twenties. Her diary was picked up by Fred Whitehurst, an American soldier. Although his job was to destroy documents of no military value, he was so moved by her writing that he decided to keep it. For more than thirty years, he hoped to return the diary to her family.
In 2005, with the help of others, Whitehurst finally achieved his goal. The diary was handed to Tram's mother in Ha Noi and was published the same year. It quickly became a bestseller and was later translated into many languages, touching readers around the world.
Today, Dang Thuy Tram is admired not only for her courage but also for her humanity. Her diary reminds young people that heroes are ordinary people who choose to serve others, and that kindness can cross even the deepest divisions between nations.

qs.p:
THE RISE OF URBAN GARDENING

In recent years, urban gardening has become increasingly popular in big cities such as Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi. Faced with limited space, many residents have turned their balconies, rooftops and even small windowsills into green areas where they grow vegetables, herbs and flowers. This trend is not merely a hobby; it reflects people's growing concern about food safety and the environment.

One major benefit of urban gardening is access to fresh, chemical-free food. Families who grow their own morning glory, tomatoes or chilies can be sure of what goes into their meals. In addition, gardening helps reduce household waste, as kitchen scraps such as eggshells and vegetable peels can be turned into compost. This natural fertiliser enriches the soil and saves money that would otherwise be spent on commercial products.

Urban gardens also bring advantages for mental health. Many people find that caring for plants helps them relax after a stressful day at work or school. Moreover, green spaces can lower the temperature of surrounding buildings, which is particularly valuable in crowded areas where concrete absorbs heat. Some apartment communities have even created shared gardens, allowing neighbours who previously hardly knew each other to cooperate and build friendships.

However, urban gardening is not without difficulties. Beginners often struggle with pests, poor sunlight or a lack of knowledge about suitable plants. To address these problems, several local organisations now offer free online courses and workshops. Experts advise newcomers to start with easy-to-grow plants like mint or green onions before attempting more demanding crops. With patience and proper guidance, almost anyone can enjoy the rewards of a small but productive garden in the middle of the city.
qs.q: According to the passage, what has made urban gardening popular?

qs.p:
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN EDUCATION

[I] Artificial intelligence (AI) is gradually changing the way students learn and teachers teach around the world. [II] Many schools in Viet Nam have begun to experiment with AI-powered applications that can assess pronunciation, correct writing errors and suggest exercises suited to each learner's level. [III] These tools provide instant feedback, which was once possible only when a teacher could spend time with each student individually. [IV] As a result, learners can practise at their own pace, even outside the classroom.

Supporters of AI argue that it can make education more personalised and accessible. A student in a remote mountainous area, for example, can use an online assistant to review difficult lessons at any time, something that would have been unimaginable a decade ago. Teachers also benefit, since automated marking frees them from repetitive tasks and gives them more time to design creative activities and support students who are falling behind.

Nevertheless, critics warn that the technology brings serious risks. Some students rely so heavily on AI to complete their assignments that they fail to develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills. There are also concerns over privacy, because educational platforms collect large amounts of personal data about young users. Furthermore, not every family can afford reliable internet access or modern devices, so the digital divide may widen rather than narrow.

To make the most of AI, educators suggest establishing clear rules for its use. Students should be taught to treat AI as a supporting tool rather than a substitute for their own effort, and they should learn to check the information it provides, since it can sometimes be inaccurate. Ultimately, technology can only improve education when it is guided by thoughtful teachers and responsible learners.
qs.q:
Where in paragraph 1 does the following sentence best fit?
"Such flexibility is especially useful for students who need extra practice."
